Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

not to mention phrase

also to say nothing of, let alone, not to mention the fact that, leaving aside

classical

Cic. Brut. 266: ut omittam cētera quae sunt innumerābilia (Lewis & Short s.v. omittō)
Cic. Cat. 3.18: ut omittam cētera (Lewis & Short s.v. cēterus)

ut omittam

purpose clause standing outside the sentence; ut omittam with the accusative, or with quod and the indicative

not to mention, to say nothing of

“That I may pass over”: the orator’s way of naming a thing while saying he will not dwell on it. The same verb in the indicative, omittō, “I say nothing of”, opens a list of things passed over.

Other words

  • ut mittam — not to mention, leaving aside

    also used · modern · Cic. Mur. 15: mittō proelia, praetereō oppugnātiōnēs oppidōrum (Lewis & Short s.v. mittō); Traupman 103: not to mention the fact that, ut mittam quod (+ indic.)

    Mittō, like omittō, means “pass over” in speaking (mittō proelia, Cic. Mur. 15); “not to mention the fact that” is ut mittam quod with the indicative. Every word is classical; we have found no classical instance of the phrase.

  • ut nihil dīcam dē (+ abl.) — not to mention

    also used · modern · Traupman 103: not to mention, ut nōn (or nihil) dīcam dē (+ abl.)

    Traupman’s phrase. Every word is classical; we have found no classical instance of the phrase. Beware nē dīcam, which is something else: “not to say”, “I might almost say”, softening a stronger word (crūdēlem Castorem, nē dīcam scelerātum, Cic. Deiot. 2, Lewis & Short s.v. crūdēlis).

Examples

  • ut mittam quod (+ indic.)

    not to mention the fact that …Traupman 345
